site_prep_notes: designed to resemble a farmers’s plot, i.e. a small area (here 5,445 m²) surrounded by primary forest, which provided the necessary shade at the beginning of plant growth; planted 605 rosewood trees in 35 rows with 3 m x 3 m spacing, with 17 trees per row (density: 1,100 trees/ha). There were three meters betweenthe external rows and the surrounding forest (trees height > 25-30 meters). The seeds originated from two different parts of East of French Guiana, half came from Cacao (4°34’60’N; 52°280’W) and half from Roura (4°43’59”N; 52°19’59”W)
veg_mgmt_notes: Nine years later, in 2011, 558 trees were still alive (8% mortality rate), and thinning was implemented by removing one out of three rows of the trees.

measurement_notes: Soil sampling was carried out on September 2009 (dry season) and April 2010 (rainy season). Each site was divided into four plots (replicates) and ten subsamples were collected in each plot (50 x 50 m) at 0-0.05, 0.05- 0.10, 0.10-0.20 and 0.20-0.40 m depth, to form a composite sample per depth. The field-moist samples were sieved (2-mm mesh) and a 300-g aliquot of each sample was separated, placed in plastic bags and stored in refrigerator at 4-8 oC for later determination of soil microbial biomass (SMB). The remaining soil samples were air-dried. Soil samples were ground and passed through a 0.21-mm sieve to determine total organic carbon (TOC) by wet combustion using a mixture of potassium dichromate and sulfuric acid under heating

prior_land_use_as_given: approximately 10-year-old regrowth forest that had grown after repeated slash-and-burn cycles for subsistence agriculture (rice—Oryza sativa, cassava—Manihot esculenta, maize—Zea mays, and cowpea—Vigna unguiculata)
tree_density_as_given: oil palm in double rows (spacing 7.5 9 9m) interspersed with strips (width 15m) consisting of nine rows of herbaceous, shrub, and tree
crop: oil palm, pigeon pea, jack bean, hemp, mucuna, sunflower, ice cream bean
site_prep_notes: in 2007 mechanical chopper pulled by tractor was used on four hectares, whereas in the remaining area (2 ha), the vegetation was chopped by hand using chainsaws and machetes. The chopped vegetation was spread on the ground to form a mulch layer. After land preparation, 1.3 Mg ha-1 of lime was applied by hand to the soil surface. In February of 2008, the intraspecific hybrid of oil palm Tenera (13-month old seedlings)was planted as the main crop of two AFSs
veg_mgmt_notes: In the other years, compost was not applied, and instead, the biomass from the management of spontaneous vegetation and pruning of the fertilizing species. consisted of removing the vegetation from around the oil palm plants (3–5 times per year), pruning old and damaged leaves (1–2 times per year), and mowing between rows (3–4 times per year). The resulting plant residues were distributed beneath the crown of oil palm seedlings and under the canopies of the other species
nutrient_notes: A mixture of Arad reactive rock phosphate and chaff charcoal (N 0.51 %; P 3.36 %; K 4.85 %; and Mg 2.7 %) was placed (10 kg plant-1) in the planting holes of the oil palm seedlings upon planting, whereas the annual maintenance fertilization (sidedressing) consisted of 8 kg of organic compost (N 1.2 %; P 0.1 %; K2O 0.4 %; and C/N 46) per plant; the organic compost contained peel, seed, and pulp residues from a local fruit pulp industry. In 2009, the sidedressing consisted of 40 kg of organic compost, 1.0 kg of bone meal (N 2 %; P2O5 20 %; K2O 0.12 %; and C/N 9), and 1.0 kg of castor cake (N 5.44 %; P2O5 1.91 %; K2O 1.54 %; and C/N 10) per plant. The final fertilization in 2010 prior to sampling supplied 0.3 kg of reactive rock phosphate, 1 kg of bone meal, and two applications of 50 kg of empty fruit bunches of oil palm per plant each. In the strips, tree seedlings were fertilized in the same manner as the oil palm seedlings at planting. In 2008, the sidedressing consisted of 10 kg of chicken manure (N 2.58 %; P2O5 2.77 %; K2O 2.31 %; and C/N 7) and 20 kg of organic compost per plant.

In February of 2008, the intraspecific hybrid of oil palm Tenera (13-month old seedlings)was planted as the main crop of two AFSs
veg_mgmt_notes: In the other years, compost was not applied, and instead, the biomass from the management of spontaneous vegetation and pruning of the fertilizing species. consisted of removing the vegetation from around the oil palm plants (3–5 times per year), pruning old and damaged leaves (1–2 times per year), and mowing between rows (3–4 times per year). nutrient_notes: A mixture of Arad reactive rock phosphate and chaff charcoal (N 0.51 %; P 3.36 %; K 4.85 %; and Mg 2.7 %) was placed (10 kg plant-1) in the planting holes of the oil palm seedlings upon planting, whereas the annual maintenance fertilization (sidedressing) consisted of 8 kg of organic compost (N 1.2 %; P 0.1 %; K2O 0.4 %; and C/N 46) per plant; the organic compost contained peel, seed, and pulp residues from a local fruit pulp industry. In February of 2008, the intraspecific hybrid of oil palm Tenera (13-month old seedlings)was planted as the main crop of two AFSs
veg_mgmt_notes: In the other years, compost was not applied, and instead, the biomass from the management of spontaneous vegetation and pruning of the fertilizing species. consisted of removing the vegetation from around the oil palm plants (3–5 times per year), pruning old and damaged leaves (1–2 times per year), and mowing between rows (3–4 times per year). The resulting plant residues were distributed beneath the crown of oil palm seedlings and under the canopies of the other species
nutrient_notes: A mixture of Arad reactive rock phosphate and chaff charcoal (N 0.51 %; P 3.36 %; K 4.85 %; and Mg 2.7 %) was placed (10 kg plant-1) in the planting holes of the oil palm seedlings upon planting, whereas the annual maintenance fertilization (sidedressing) consisted of 8 kg of organic compost (N 1.2 %; P 0.1 %; K2O 0.4 %; and C/N 46) per plant; the organic compost contained peel, seed, and pulp residues from a local fruit pulp industry. In 2009, the sidedressing consisted of 40 kg of organic compost, 1.0 kg of bone meal (N 2 %; P2O5 20 %; K2O 0.12 %; and C/N 9), and 1.0 kg of castor cake (N 5.44 %; P2O5 1.91 %; K2O 1.54 %; and C/N 10) per plant. The final fertilization in 2010 prior to sampling supplied 0.3 kg of reactive rock phosphate, 1 kg of bone meal, and two applications of 50 kg of empty fruit bunches of oil palm per plant each. In the strips, tree seedlings were fertilized in the same manner as the oil palm seedlings at planting. In 2008, the sidedressing consisted of 10 kg of chicken manure (N 2.58 %; P2O5 2.77 %; K2O 2.31 %; and C/N 7) and 20 kg of organic compost per plant.

site_prep_notes: the natural forest was cleared by removing large trees by chainsaw and burning the remaining vegetation
veg_mgmt_notes: sown with rice, soybean, and then grass species
nutrient_notes: Limestone was applied to raise base saturation to 50% and superphosphate was added at the rate of 150 kg ha-1. In the beginning of the rainy season (October–November), rice (Oryza sativa L.) was planted between the rows after applying 300 kg ha-1 of fertilizer (NPK 5–25–15). After rice harvest (mechanical) in Year 1, soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] was grown between tree rows with fertilizer application (NPK, 2–30–15) of 450 kg ha-1. Zinc (zinc sulfate), boron (boric acid), cobalt (cobalt sulfate), and molybdenum (sodium molybdate) were applied as one-time-only applications at rates of 10, 1, 2, and 1 kg ha-1, respectively. In the third year, seeds of the grass species (Brachiaria brizantha cv. Marandu) were sown at the beginning of the rainy season between the eucalyptus rows, with fertilizer application of 150 and 200 kg ha-1 of superphosphate and phosphate rock, respectively and urea at the rate of 75 kg N ha-1
animal_notes: Animals were allowed to graze the area 90 d after sowing grass seeds; the average animal stocking rates were 0.6 and 2.5 animal ha-1 in the dry and wet seasons, respectively

prior_land_use_as_given: was managed as a single pasture that was grazed by sheep each springsummer from the 1950’s until 1977. Grazing pressurewas moderate with approximately half of each year’s 2000 to 3000 kg ha–1 annual herbage production consumed by sheep. Pasture vegetation was primarily naturalized annual grasses together with planted perennial pasture species, such as tall oatgrass Arrhenatherum elatius, L, Presel., perennial ryegrass Lolium perenne L., and burnet Sanguisorba inor, Scop.. The entire site was plowed and used to grow winter wheat during 1978 and 1979. Approximately 150 kg ha–1 of N as ammonium nitrate fertilizer was applied to the wheat crops in 1978 and again in 1979. It was allowed to return to pasture in 1980, but grazing by sheep was light and infrequent. By 1988, cool season annual grasses, tall oatgrass, and burnet again dominated the site
site_prep_notes: established in 1988-1989. Treatment plots were randomly assigned within upper-, mid-, and lower-slope blocks. Pastures and agroforests were planted with 9 kg ha–1 of Rhizobium inoculated sub-clover Trifolium subterraneum L. var. Nangeela in September 1988.
nutrient_notes: none
animal_notes: Pasture and agroforest plots were individually fenced with electric fencing in March 1990. They were grazed twice each year during 1990-2000, once in April to early-May when forage standing crops exceeded 1500 kg ha–1 and again in mid-June to early- July when forage standing crops exceeded 3000 kg/ ha–1. Grazing was timed to end in July, when stored soil moisture is exhausted and forage growth on hill pastures ends. Sufficient ewes were introduced in each plot to consume approximately half of the forage standing crop within 2-5 days. This generally resulted in stocking densities of 200-400 sheep ha–1 and residue stubble heights of 2-5 cm.

site_prep_notes: established as an experiment in 1982
veg_mgmt_notes: Complete shoot pruning occurred twice a year, prunings applied to the soil once per crop (twice a year total), ploughed to 20 cm before each crop
nutrient_notes: Mineral fertiliser (NH4NO3) was used from 1982 to 1995, but since then it was replaced with chicken manure to address soil P deficiency. Additions of mineral fertiliser and chicken manure occurred at a rate of 50 kgN/ha/yr for bean crops and 100 kgN/ha/yr for maize crops. Analysis of the chicken manure showed an average nutrient content of 2.72% N, 2.48% P, 2.81% K, 0.95% Mg and 10.17% Ca and was added at an annual rate of 5520 kg/ha dry weight

site_prep_notes: use the traditional Maresha plow to prepare their farm for maize production. The plowing system is simple and shallow tilling up to soil depth of 15 cm on average. local farmers have to do repeated tillage with any two consecutive tillage operations carried out perpendicular to each other. As a result, the soil is pulverized resulting in weak soil structure and compact formation.
veg_mgmt_notes: often remove maize residues after harvest either for fuel wood or animal feed. Thus, no crop residue remains in the field each season for either mulching or organic amendment to the soil
nutrient_notes: have access to commercial fertilizers and sometimes use manure and compost in their farm plots near to their homesteads. DAP (diammonium phosphate, (NH4)2HPO4) was used simultaneously at the time of sowing maize. On the other hand, Urea (with 6% of Nitrogen) was used after the crop develops 2–3 leaves.

veg_mgmt_notes: Farmers gather leaves and feed to cattle. At the end of fallow, farmers cut the Leucaena trees with a machete to clear the field for agricultural crops. Farmers do not bum after clearing. Instead, they drive about 30-cm long stakes of Leucaena into the ground at regular intervals long the contours. Then they pile the smaller branches (maximum of about 2 em diameter) on the upper slope side of the stake so that a fascine-like structure is formed. Fascines are bundles of long and dense brushwood of varying length used for slope stabilization which means obstruction
nutrient_notes: During the third year of cultivation it was observed that farmers apply a small amount of chicken manure (we were not able to determine the exact amount). This could be an additional reason why farmers are able to maintain high yield levels. Typically, no chemical fertilizers are applied

During winter, cover crops (mainly yellow mustard (Sinapis alba L.) and perennial and Italian ryegrass (Lolium perenne L. and Lolium multiflorum Lam.)) are applied
nutrient_notes: Fields are fertilised with animal manure in accordance with Flemish manure regulations (max rate of 170 kg N [ha yr]-1 for maize, potatoes, and winter cereals when combined with cover crops, and limitation of P addition as required by VLM, 2014). Additional mineral fertilisation was applied according to crop requirements set forth by VLM (2014) and the Bemex expert system (Vandendriessche et al., 1996)

prior_land_use_as_given: unimproved pasture for four or five years prior to hedgerows, previously sorghum-bean-maize rotation
site_prep_notes: shrubs/weeds removed with hand tools three weeks before planting in 1991. Soil prepared to 25 cm, 30 cm wide. Seeds were not inoculated before planting
veg_mgmt_notes: first weeding took place three weeks after planting using hand tools, later weedings done every 45-day. Following establishment (~11 months after planting), hedgerows pruned to 50 cm three to four times a year and leaf and stems applied to soil. Stems larger than 1 cm were placed next to hedegrows to increase barrier effect.
nutrient_notes: prunings applied to soil

prior_land_use_as_given: Deforestation in the region peaked in mid-20th century for cattle production and coffee plantations (Leonidio 2009), and pasturelands on flat topography have been rapidly replaced by sugarcane plantations in the last decade; Brazilian NGO “Instituto de Pesquisas Ecológicas” (IPE) started restoration and agroforestry projects in the region in order to promote social development in land-reform settlements and conservation of the highly threatened species
site_prep_notes: All agroforests were about 1 ha in size, established in small farms within rural settlements (Fig. 1), and consisted essentially of two planting rows of coffee (Coffea arabica L., varieties Obata and IPR 100) alternating with one row of Atlantic Forest native trees. Native trees were randomly selected.
veg_mgmt_notes: In some cases, farmers abandoned agroforests after the first few years and left the area only for forest protection, increasing mortality of coffee plants. and weeded through mowing and/or glyphosate spraying
nutrient_notes: and fertilized in the first 2 years after planting
animal_notes: were fenced to prevent cattle invasion
measurement_notes: median, biomass value may or may not include coffee given the min_dbh of 5

planted to 50 cm depth using an auger (15 cm diameter) mounted on a tractor. After planting, auger holes were filled with soil that was gradually compacted with a stud. veg_mgmt_notes: June of the first two growing seasons, competing vegetation was treated with a spot herbicide application of glyphosate (1 m2/tree).
animal_notes: early June 2011, the experimental design was protected from deer with a 250 cm tall plastic fence that was erected around each block

site_prep_notes: Site preparation included disking and subsoiling to facilitate planting in spring 1995
veg_mgmt_notes: A combination of chemical (Sulfometuron methyl and Glyphosate) and mechanical (mowing and manual pulling) treatments were used for weed control during the first and second growing seasons
nutrient_notes: Fertilization at the time of planting included broadcast application of diammonium phosphate,dolomitic lime, potash, and a micronutrient mixture. These treatments added elemental calcium, nitrogen, phosphorous, magnesium, zinc, copper, and manganese (1,008, 50, 56, 125, 3.4, 3.4, and 2.2 kg/ ha , respectively). Soil pH was adjusted to 6.0 with 3,362 kg ha of dolomitic lime. No subsequent fertilizer

prior_land_use_as_given: In August 1980 one hectare of upland soils (Typic Paleudult) was cleared with a D7 bulldozer which a straight blade that mixed the thin layer of topsoil with the acidic subsoil (20–40 cm) and compacted the soil (Alegre et al.,1988). Thereafter only one season of rice was sown. The results obtained were very poor and the field site was abandoned until August 1982
site_prep_notes: On November 1982, peach palm was planted
veg_mgmt_notes: During 1986 and part of 1987 the peach palm plantation was managed in the traditional fashion palm trees with a natural grass understorey, initially planted with 1200 but then thinned to 600 trees/ha. October 1988, when each palm was 6 years old, inoculated seed of centrosema was sown as an understorey cover with a spacing of 1 m between rows and 0.50 m between plants. About 20% of the area needed gap filling which was done a month after initial sowing
nutrient_notes: applying different rates of N, P, and K, for three years. Due to low content of nutrients in the soil (Table 1), 20 kg of P ha–1 as Bayovar rock phosphate and 20 kg K ha as potassium chloride were spread over the entire area in May 1989. These are the recommended rates of fertilizer for establishing new pastures, which would also be adequate for recouperation of degraded pastures
animal_notes: Eighteen months after the establishment of centrosema, grazing commenced with two young bulls of 180 and 171 kg each, at a stocking rate of 3.3 animals/ha. A rotational grazing system was used, with 9 to 14 days grazing periods and 28 to 30 days rest according to the size of the plots. Subsequently the stocking rate was reduced to 2.3 animals/ha because of the decreased availability of centrosema biomass during the dry season and to allow for recouperation of Centrosema. The cattle received an additional salt/mineral supplement

site_prep_notes: Seeds were sown directly in black polythene tubes (15 10 cm, height and diameter, respectively) after immersion for 1 min in boiling (100 °C) water. The soil mixture consisted of sandy clay loam, forest clay loam and sand at the atio of 3:1:1 as recommended by Tanzania Forestry Research Institute. The seeds were sown at a depth of 5 mm in polythene tubes which were placed on prepared seed beds under a grass shed and watered twice daily with an overhead sprinkler to facilitate seed germination. The seedlings were also watered twice daily in the morning and afternoon. This was reduced to once a day 2 weeks prior to planting. The tubes were maintained weed-free and the roots were pruned when they penetrated into the nursery bed soil. The seedlings were raised in the nursery for 65 days
veg_mgmt_notes: plots kept weed free
nutrient_notes: At planting, phosphorus was mixed into the hole of each seedling at the rate of 9 kg P/ha as triple superphosphate.

measurement_notes: In June 2009, a trench measuring 0.5 x 1.2 x 1.2m (width x length x depth) was dug per plot in each treatment (Figure 4). On the walls of the trench, deformed and undeformed soil samples were collected at depths of 0-5, 5-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-50 cm. Carbon stock was calculated for the sum of the samples from each trench, i.e., the total contained from 0 to 50 cm. The deformed samples were used for chemical analysis, while the undeformed samples were used for soil density determination. In May 2009, 8 single deformed soil samples were also collected with an auger along a transect in each plot at depths 0-5, 5-10, 10-20, 20-30 and 30-50 cm (Figure 5). The single samples were pooled to form one composite sample per plot. The composite samples were air-dried, sieved on 2 mm mesh and stored in plastic bags for further chemical analysis. To calculate the soil carbon stock, the carbon concentration and soil density data obtained for each sample in all treatments were used.

management_notes: The sampling of leaf litter was carried out randomly, in one of the two 1000 m2 MTPs. Five subsamples of leaf litter were taken, without including weeds or other material that was not leaf litter, through a 0.5x0.5 m frame. They were mixed and weighed to obtain the total fresh weight, then a sample of approximately 250 g was taken and sent to the laboratory of the Universidad Centroamérica (UCA), duly labeled and sealed in a plastic bag, to obtain the dry weight of the sample at 75°C and determine the percentage of dry matter. The samples were kept in the oven for 24 to 72 hours until a constant dry weight was obtained.

prior_land_use_as_given: continuously cropped for 50 years, then fallowed for two years before experiment started
site_prep_notes: received randomly but equally spaced plantings of G. senegalensis seedlings that resulted in a density of 1521 plants ha
veg_mgmt_notes: coppicing in late April or May before crops, followed by one or two more coppicings during the growing season, shrub residues were cut into 5–10-cm pieces and spread evenly over the soil surface, millet planted on odd year, groundnut on even year, fallowed between 2007 to 2010, then cropping began again in 2011, cultivation closely followed the local subsistence farmer practices that was done manually and with animal traction that included pre-planting shallow tillage sweep cultivator to a depth of 10–15 cm) to prepare the seedbed. Weeding was done periodically during the rainy season by hand hoeing and using a shallow cultivator drawn by horses
nutrient_notes: Beginning in 2003, millet (var Souna 3) was planted in all plots and fertilized with 68.5 kg N, 15 kg P, and 15 kg K ha􀀀 1 to allow plots one year to equilibrate before data collection began the following year.
measurement_notes: Using the bulk density to calculate C to a depth of 10 cm at the end of 2015, there was 3700 more kg ha of total C in the +shrub plots than in the –shrub plots (6667 compared to 2952 kg ha total C). Without fertilizer addition, the difference was 3229 kg ha more total C.

site_prep_notes: Strips of pasture grass into which the trees were planted were treated with glyphosate (Roundup) herbicide at the time of establishment
veg_mgmt_notes: pesticides applied on the farm have included Commence (chlomazone) in 1989 and 1991, Extrazine (atrazine and cyanazine) in 1990, 1992, 1993, and 1994 and Eradicane (EPTC) in 1990 and 1992, 50% of the dogwood seedlings died and replaced by viburnum and Nanking cherry. Poplar survival was adversely influenced on plot 12 by the two major floods of 1990 and 1991. Seedlings in over one-half of the plot were washed away in 1990 and the replanted seedlings were washed away again in 1991
nutrient_notes: During the past twelve years, impregnated urea pellets have been applied at the rate of 134 kg ha-'. On legume fields, 90 kg ha -1 of 120-60-60 (N-P-K) are applied annually
animal_notes: Until 1988, livestock also were allowed to graze along parts of the creek riparian zone, which caused severe stream bank erosion and impacted the riparian plant and animal community (riparian buffer established 1990)
measurement_notes: since kg/tree, density is for trees only but there are 1000 additional shrubs

Additionally, “efficient microorganisms” ((EM) this amendment contains 4.2% humic acids and 5.0% fulvic acids) are incorporated; the additional composition is 1.3% N; 1.2% P; 2.4% K; 2.2% Ca; 1.7% Mg; 0.02% Mn; and 0.02% B. The EM is applied t the foliar level, monthly, at a rate of one liter of EM in 200 L water (this volume supplies 50 avocado plants and 900 coffee trees).

prior_land_use_as_given: row crops, such as corn and soybeans, were grown on the land for many years. The area was in field corn, sweet corn, and oats before the project was started in 1986
site_prep_notes: More than 1.2 ha were disced and planted to oats in spring 1986. Just before planting, 1.4 ha of the site, including the 1.2 ha oats, were disced again. The planting site was rototilled with a farm tractor and a power-take-off-driven unit on the day of planting
veg_mgmt_notes: 3 to 5 year rotation, Pre-emergent herbicidces were applied after planting. For the two Populus clones, Goal and Surflan were tank-mixed and applied broadcast. Princep, Goal, and Surflan were used for the silver maple seedlings. Subsequent growth of tree crowns was sufficient to rely only on mowing to control weeds. In 1986, Surflan, Goal, and Princep were applied to the silver maple plots, and Surflan and Goal were applied to the Populus clones. In 1987, Surflan was the only herbicide used because of labeling restrictions with Princep and the desire to reduce chemical inputs. Although the 1987 herbicide costs were lower, the weed competition for those plots was severe. Mechanical mowing has not been an effective control method on these plantings. During the summer of 1987, an outbreak of cottonwood leaf beetle (Chrysomela scripta) threatened to defoliate the plantation. A chemical application of Sevin was used to successfully control the beetle.
nutrient_notes: Given the previous agronomic cropping with customary applications of N and the assumed high natural fertility of the soils, no additional nutrients were applied to the approximately 3.4 ha planting site

site_prep_notes: seeds were hand-scarified by nicking with a knife and inoculated with Rhizobia NGR 8 (Nitragin Co., Milwaukee, Wisconsin, U.S.A.). The seeds were germinated in 3.8 × 3.8 by 38-cm cardboard con tainers (Monarch, Salida, Colorado) in late October, 1983. Each container was filled with a peat, perlite, and vermiculite soil mix that was amended with macro- and micronutrients. The seedlings were grown in a greenhouse for 5 months until out-planting in the field on 22 March 1984. The soil was turned over with a moldboard plow and further broken up with a olling cultivator. Oryzalin (Surflan), a pre-plant herbicide, was incorporated into the soil 1 day prior to planting at a rate of 2.8 kg ha- 1
veg_mgmt_notes: In the first year, while the trees were less than 1.2 m tall, mechanical weed control was provided in both spacings with a sweep cultivator. This device passed over the tops of the trees and provided 1 m of cultivation on both sides of the row. In addition, a 2-m-wide disk harrow pulled by a 20-kw tractor was used to provide weed control in the 3-m-wide spacing. The 3-m-wide spacing also permitted use of a 20-kw tractor and spray rig for herbicide application. All trees were hand-weeded 8 weeks after planting in 1984. Dead trees were manually replanted and 12 weeks after the initial planting. In the second and third growing-season, a mix of oryzalin and trifluralin (2.8 kg ha-I and 2.2 kg ha -1, respectively) was applied in the 1.5 X 3.0-m spacings for weed control.
nutrient_notes: Liquid ammonium phosphate fertilizer (10-34-0) at a rate of 176 kg ha- 1 was sprayed into the furrow created by the heavy-duty forestry-type tree planter (Felker et al., 1986) during the transplanting operation. This was the only fertilizer used during the study period

site_prep_notes: planted in September, 1989. trees were planted in 20-cm wide and 100–120-cm deep holes dug out with tractor-mounted post-hole digger
nutrient_notes: These augerholes were refilled with a mixture of original dug out soil plus 3 kg gypsum and 8 kg farm manure in each augerhole. Inter-row space was amended with gypsum equivalent to gypsum requirement of the soil before the first intercrop was planted in the summer (kharif season) of 1990. Crops were fertilized depending on crop: rice (150 kgN/ha, 50 kg ZnSO4/ha), wheat (120 kgN/ha, 50 kg P2O5/ha), berseem (15 kgN/ha, 50 kg P2O5/ha), mustard (15 kgN/ha, 40 kg P2O5/ha), pigeonpea (15 kgN/ha, 40 kg P2O5/ha), sorghum (100 kgN/ha), tumeric (200 kgN/ha, 60 to 25 kg P2O5/ha, 25 ZnSO4), oats (120 kgN/ha, 50 kg P2O5/ha), guinea grass (75 kgN/ha), cowpea (20 kgN/ha, 55 kg P2O5/ha)
measurement_notes: Soil values appear to be average over all understorey crop treatments; recorded as separate plotIDs

irrigation_notes: For establishment of saplings, three irrigations with 10 cm depth of water were applied monthly during the first year after planting and thereafter once annually in June
measurement_notes: assuming no animals since they specify fodder for all removed grasses

site_prep_notes: Site preparation included ploughing and disking each abandoned farmland site in fall 1999, to physically enhance soil conditions and facilitate plantation the following spring. In the spring of 2000, bare-root stocks with 2 m-long stems were planted manually with shovels
veg_mgmt_notes: None of the planted poplar clones were protected against deer browsing with fences or chemical deterrents. Competing vegetation was eliminated with glyphosate herbicide application over the entire plantation area in June 2000, and between plantation rows only in June 2001. In 2007, one tree per plot was harvested at the end of the 8th growing season to develop allometric relationships and evaluate plantation yields
nutrient_notes: Neither lime nor fertilizer applications (organic or chemical) were made before or during the course of the study

site_prep_notes: In 2004 land preparation commenced to install two long term cacao management treatments. Under thinned native forest. weeds and shrubs were removed manually and the native tree density was selectively reduced by cutting uneconomical trees to achieve approximately 50% shade.
veg_mgmt_notes: Hand weeding with machete as needed. IPM are referred to integrated pest management that consist in the optimization of cultural practices [15], such as removal of sick and diseases infested parts of the tree, adequate pruning,and protection of pods with cooper fungicide in the period of pod development (four times per year between December to March). Pruning one time a year.
nutrient_notes: At planting 250 g seabirds manure, mixed with inorganic fertilizer 0.5 kg (14N-12P-4K) was added to each pit. Mineral fertilization 0.5 kg of 196 N -250P-220K (urea, Diammoium phosphate, Potassium chloride) per plant at 2010

nutrient_notes: no fertilizer

site_prep_notes: For planting, seminal seedlings of Pinus caribaea var. hondurensis, from the Pomar Clonal of the company Duratex S/A. site_prep_notes: Each plot was planted in 2011 with 6 m × 3 cm diameter poplar poles obtained from the GreenWood Resources Inc., Nursery, Boardman Tree Farm, Boardman, OR
veg_mgmt_notes: Switchgrass was harvested annually in early July (1–8 July) and October (1–5 October) each year with a Hesston discbine swather (AGCO Corporation, Duluth, GA). Following cutting and before windrowing the switchgrass hay was aerated to speed drying with up to five passes of a New Holland tedder (New Holland Agriculture). The hay was then bailed with a Case International Harvester 8555 baler (Racine, WI) and removed from the field. Weeds were controlled annually with glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] at 13.0 g a.i./ha in late March during switchgrass dormancy
nutrient_notes: All monoculture and intercropped switchgrass plots, received a blended dry granular fertilizer of 112 kg N/ha as urea (45–0–0), 28 kg P/ha as mono-ammonium phosphate (11–52–0), 112 kg K/ha as potash (0–0–60), and 56 kg S/ha as ammonium sulfate (21–0–24) in April and 112 kg N/ha as urea after the first harvest in July each year with a 3 m (width) Barber spreader (Barber Engineering Company, Spokane, WA)
irrigation_notes: Irrigation was applied by solid set sprinklers positioned within the tree rows. Rain gauges were placed in each plot to quantify the amount of water applied over the growing season. The cumulative amount and duration of irrigation applied during the season was managed by Greenwood Resources Inc. with an average of 225 cm/ha from April to October in the establishment year and increased to 300 cm/ha by year four of the study determined from the rain gauge data
measurement_notes: allometric equation not publicaly available (pers. comm)

Merryll) was grown in the summer season of 2009/10, Sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea) was grown in winter-spring of 2010 and maize (Zea mays) was grown in association with palisade grass (Urochloa brizantha cv. animal_notes: Freshly weaned beef cattle were introduced in September 2011 at a stocking rate of 4.4 heads per hectare weighting 174 kg on average, and grown up to slaughtering in June 2014, weighting 492 kg on average, in a continuous grazing system. After the slaughter of the first batch a ew batch of freshly weaned beef cattle was introduced at a stocking rate of 3.2 heads per hectare, weighting 179 kg on average, in September 2014, and kept up to the end of the experiment, when the average weigh was 342 kg

site_prep_notes: At the beginning of March 2002, the seeds were soaked and inoculated with bacteria of the genus Rhyzobium. The following day, the seeds were sown in 300- cm3 containers filled with Spagnum peat:vermiculite (3:1 vol ratio). After three months in a nurs ery,in the first week of June, the seedlings were planted in the field. Soil was prepred with eradication of pre-existing vegetation, followed by a deep ripping at 50 cm and a shallow tillage.
veg_mgmt_notes: Weeds were manually controlled during the first year. From the second year on wards,weed control was unnecessary because of the high cultivation density and the rapid growth of the new sprouts. Cut every three years
nutrient_notes: Standard fertilization before planting with N (160 kg h) K (110 kg ha), P (19 kg ha), and Mg (12 kg ha), equivalent to a 113-9 ratio fertilizer (N–P2O5–K2O), plus 1,4 MgO. Thereafter, no fertilizer was added,
irrigation_notes: Irrigation was applied only during the first three months after planting to ensure plant survival. Irrigation amounted to 54 mm (4.5 mm per week) from late June to mid- September.

site_prep_notes: Ploughing was done in between the hedgerows using a tractor on the contours across the slope. The plough depth was maintained as 0.2 m.
veg_mgmt_notes: hedge row trees were pruned before crop cultivation 0.5 m above ground level and all the pruned leafy materials were separated from branches and incorporated into the soil after measuring their respective treatment during ploughing.
nutrient_notes: Prior to planting the first year, the experiment site received a uniform application of 2 Mg/ha of well decomposed farm yard manure (FYM), 30 kg/ha of urea, 60 kg/ha of di-ammoniumphosphate (DAP), and 40 kg/ha of muriate of potash (MOP). After the first manual hand weeding (around 30 days after sowing), the plots were top dressed with 65 kg/ha of urea. second year onwards, only 50% of the above fertilizer application was used in addition to incorporation of leafy pruning material of the respective treatments.

site_prep_notes: established 2011, Before planting, soil preparation and the eradication of pre-existing weeds consisted of a deep plowing at 50 cm, shallow tillage (harrowing), pre-emergent herbicide application (Oxifluorfen 24%, 2.5 L ha), Bare root nursery seedlings, 50–70 cm in length, of two Robinia pseudoacacia L. taxa (the improved cultivar “Nyírségi” and commercial nursery plants from Germany), Populus nigra L., Ailanthus altissima (Mill) Swingle., and Ulmus pumila L; Paulownia plants of 15–20 cm in height (Paulownia fortunei (Seem.) Hemsl., clone “UHU”) coming from root cuttings; Bare root nursery plants, 50–70 cm in length, coming from rooted hardwood cuttings of Platanus hispanica Mill. ex Münchh; Poplar hardwood cuttings of 20–25 cm in length belonging to five hybrid clones—four clones of Populus x euroamericana (Dode) Guinier (clones “Adige”, “AF2”, “Oudenberg”, “I214”), and one clone of Populus interamericana van Broekhuizen (clone “Raspalje”).
veg_mgmt_notes: 4 year rotations, 2 rotations, Weeds were mechanically controlled again three months after planting, but fortunately it was unnecessary to control them thereafter, due to the high planting density and the rapid growth of the new sprouts after harvesting, in the Mo1 and Mo2 trials, occasionally during the whole period studied (only in two years) a pest caused by Xanthogaleruca luteola that affected Ulmus pumila had to be controlled, by spraying 0.5 L ha of Deltamethrin at 2.5% every time
nutrient_notes: before planting standard fertilization with N (75 kg h), K (62.3 kg ha), P (32.7 kg ha) and S (24 kg ha) corresponding to a 15–15–15 (12 S) ratio fertilizer (N–P2O5–K2O plus 12 SO3); fertilizers were added by fertigation: N (50 kg h year); K (41.5 kg ha yr); P (21.8 kg ha yr); S (16.0 kg ha yr); and 3 kg ha year of Fe–Zn–Mn (4.5%–1.5%–0.5%) chelated by EDDHA, 100 g ha yr of Cu (14%) chelated by EDTA, 50 g ha of H3BO3 and 5 g ha year of (NH4)2MoO4. Sulfur was supplied for facilitating the absorption of Fe, Zn and Mn, since they seem to be somewhat locked-away from plants, as symptoms of foliar interveinal chlorosis were observed
irrigation_notes: Every year, from early June to mid-September and according to the rainfall, 160–480 mm of water was supplied by drip irrigation in order to offset summer drought and achieve an annual water supply (rainfall + irrigation) of around 700–800 mm

veg_mgmt_notes: 4 year rotations, 2 rotations, Weeds were mechanically controlled again three months after planting, but fortunately it was unnecessary to control them thereafter, due to the high planting density and the rapid growth of the new sprouts after harvesting, in the Mo1 and Mo2 trials, occasionally during the whole period studied (only in two years) a pest caused by Xanthogaleruca luteola that affected Ulmus pumila had to be controlled, by spraying 0.5 L ha of Deltamethrin at 2.5% every time
nutrient_notes: before planting standard fertilization with N (75 kg h), K (62.3 kg ha), P (32.7 kg ha) and S (24 kg ha) corresponding to a 15–15–15 (12 S) ratio fertilizer (N–P2O5–K2O plus 12 SO3); fertilizers were added by fertigation: N (50 kg h year); K (41.5 kg ha yr); P (21.8 kg ha yr); S (16.0 kg ha yr); and 3 kg ha year of Fe–Zn–Mn (4.5%–1.5%–0.5%) chelated by EDDHA, 100 g ha yr of Cu (14%) chelated by EDTA, 50 g ha of H3BO3 and 5 g ha year of (NH4)2MoO4. Sulfur was supplied for facilitating the absorption of Fe, Zn and Mn, since they seem to be somewhat locked-away from plants, as symptoms of foliar interveinal chlorosis were observed
irrigation_notes: Every year, from early June to mid-September and according to the rainfall, 160–480 mm of water was supplied by drip irrigation in order to offset summer drought and achieve an annual water supply (rainfall + irrigation) of around 700–800 mm

veg_mgmt_notes: Plots were kept weed-free by manual hoeing. Cowpea was protected against insects by spraying with insecticide (Abamectine 18 g/L and Deltam´ethrine 25 g/L) at least twice during the cropping season. nutrient_notes: small doses of various fertilizers each year that did not impact SOC

site_prep_notes: the two blocks were plowed each season by animal traction at 15 cm depth. Millet was sown each year after the first 20 mm rain in the growing season. Several seeds were planted per hill to allow subsequent thinning one week after planting at three plants per hill. Cowpea was sown 15 days after millet, and it was also thinned one week later at two plants per hill

animal_notes: The experimental area was divided into fifteen paddocks. of 310 m2, in order to establish a rotational grazing cycle of 22.5 days (1.5 days of occupation and 21 days Rest). The total experimental area was 4650 m2, with a forage availability of grasses of around 1200 to 1300 kg DM ha-1 year-1.

site_prep_notes: planted in 1995
veg_mgmt_notes: Initially intercropped with cereal and legume crops. Since 2010, the site has been owned by market-gardeners using organic farming practices and the trees have been intercropped with vegetables. Trees were strongly pruned in February 2015 and again in February 2018 in this treatment to obtain pollarded trees. Crop alleys have been cultivated with a rotation of carrots, tomatoes and lettuces since 2015. Raised beds were mechanically refreshed (rotary tilled and formed) in March and covered with a 2 to 3 cm thick ramial chipped wood layer obtained from walnut prunings
nutrient_notes: received two top dressings of poultry manure for a total of 56 g/m2 once after raised beds were formed, and a second time when tomatoes were planted

site_prep_notes: From each provenance approximately 2 kg drupe was collected during October November (2012), brought to laboratory for further analysis and processing. The C. australis ripened drupe was dried under the sun for 24 h. The seed of each source was stored in the refrigerator during winter (NoveJan), and subsequently it was sown in the nursery during the first week of February 2013. The C. australis seeds were soaked in water for 24 h before sowing in the nursery to hasten the germination process. Hundred seeds of each seed-source were sown in polybag to grow seedling in the nursery. In December (2013), six-month-old nursery grown saplings of C. australis were planted

veg_mgmt_notes: performed minimal tillage (plowing at 15 cm) on all plots only at the beginning of the experiment in early March 2017 and did not till the soils in the following two years. According to local farmers, pruning mulberry trees every year in December is a common practice. Generally, the farmers prune the mulberry trees to approximately 40 cm from ground level and remove the pruned materials from the plot. They also typically leave mustard residues in the field after harvest because the roots and leaves can function as green manure for the next crop after fermentation and decay. Moreover, to avoid the adverse effects of herbicide and pesticide use on the soil environment and soil characteristics, manual weeding and pest control measures were carried out in the plots
nutrient_notes: At planting, inorganic fertilizers such as N, P, and K were applied according to the conventional application rates used by local farmers. site_prep_notes: Six-month-old healthy seedlings (uniform size) of G. arborea were planted
veg_mgmt_notes: The multiple stemmed plants were pruned to single stem one year after planting. The weeds were removed in 1-year-old stands by tilling and hoeing, while in 2- and 3-year-old stands sporadic weed patches were controlled by spot application of herbicides and hoeing. In the remaining age series (4-, 5- and 6-year-old plantations), weeds were controlled by tilling with a tractor twice during monsoon and summer.
nutrient_notes: A pre planting fertilizer dose of 100 kg ha N, 40 kg ha P, and 80 kg ha K was applied. Additional nitrogen was applied at 120 kg ha in two split doses (in July and March) in 1-year-old stands. No fertilizers were applied after 1 year of planting
irrigation_notes: Plantations were irrigated at a weekly interval in summer (March–June) and at a monthly interval in winter (October–February), while no irrigation was provided in the rainy season (July– September). The total water irrigated averaged 600–800 mm per annum

Goal 2XL (2 L ha and Simazine 480 (4.7 L ha). site_prep_notes: Coffee planting takes place between May to July
veg_mgmt_notes: Shade trees not yet pruned. Pruning of coffee takes place between January and August, when farmers weed and clean fields, remove dead trees and prune coffee bushes. Between March and May, farmers prune shade trees, particularly leguminous species such as Inga sp. and Erythrina poeppigiana.Pesticides are applied to coffee farms several times a year to limit the incidence of pests. Coffee harvesting takes place between September and December, depending on local conditions and annual climate
nutrient_notes: Fertilizers are applied three times per year – May, June and November – to coincide with the flowering, fruiting and post-harvest stages of production. Pruned branches left on soil as fertilizer

All cropping plots (with or without trees) received a basal fertilizer application of 45 kg ha"1 of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (i.e. 300 kg ha"1 of compound fertilizer NPK 15:15:15) during the main cropping season of 1983. This rate was increased to 60 kg N ha"1 in the main season in 1984. In 1985 and 1986 (Period II) calcium ammonium nitrate (26% N) was applied at a rate of 45 kg N ha"1 to all cropped plots in the main season. One third of the fertilizer was broadcast at planting, and the remainder side-dressed after four or five weeks. Throughout the trial, no fertilizer was applied during the minor season to enable assessment of residual effects in the various cropping treatments.

veg_mgmt_notes: During the cropping periods, the trees were maintained as hedgerows, and pruned four or five times each year to a height of about 50 cm. This minimized shading of the associated arable crops in the alleys and at the same time provided prunings on a regular basis for mulch and organic manure for the alley crops. Trees in the grazing plots were cut less frequently and therefore grew bigger than those under alley cropping. During Period I, trees in the two grazing treat mentswere not cut at all in 1983 and therefore had two full years growth prior to their first cutting in April 1984, with a second cutting in October of the same year. These two cuttings were maintained during Period II, but with alternate rows of trees being cut every third month (equivalent to two cuttings per year for each row). This alternate cutting arrangement ensured adequate light penetration to the undergrowth for the grazing animals. Also, trees in the grazing plots were cut to a height of 1.5 m instead of 0.5 m as in the cropped plots, to prevent young shoot regrowths from being grazed by the sheep.

animal_notes: Grazing was on a two-day rotation basis (two days grazing, followed by 22 days rest). The total grazing area was 0.144 ha (120 X 12 m) and the number of animals grazing this area varied from two to six depending on time of year (dry or wet season) and the availability of herbage within the grazing plots. This minimized shading of the associated arable crops in the alleys and at the same time provided prunings on a regular basis for mulch and organic manure for the alley crops. Trees in the grazing plots were cut less frequently and therefore grew bigger than those under alley cropping. During Period I, trees in the two grazing treat mentswere not cut at all in 1983 and therefore had two full years growth prior to their first cutting in April 1984, with a second cutting in October of the same year. These two cuttings were maintained during Period II, but with alternate rows of trees being cut every third month (equivalent to two cuttings per year for each row). This alternate cutting arrangement ensured adequate light penetration to the undergrowth for the grazing animals. Also, trees in the grazing plots were cut to a height of 1.5 m instead of 0.5 m as in the cropped plots, to prevent young shoot regrowths from being grazed by the sheep.
